en: [1] That which is without beginning or end, peaceful, the exhaustion of existence and non-existence, all-pervading, and inseparable from emptiness and compassion—this is known as *bodhicitta*.

[2] Having prostrated with my whole being to that jewel of reality, great bliss, which is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, Vajragarbha writes this down. [3] In the fifth chapter, the commentator shall teach the reality of Buddhahood for the benefit of all sentient beings, so that they may attain the fruit of Mahāmudrā.

Regarding this, the Blessed One said: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the Chapter on Reality. By the words beginning with "in its own nature," the essential nature is elaborated; it is the self-cognizing gnosis of the Tathāgata.

In that essential nature, which is free from the eighteenfold transformations of the grasped, the act of grasping, and the grasper, there is no external form for yogins, no seer, and no visual consciousness;
likewise, no sound, no hearer, and no auditory consciousness;
likewise, no odor, no smeller, and no olfactory consciousness.
Likewise, there is no taste, no taster, and no tongue-consciousness;
similarly, there is no touch, no toucher, and no body-consciousness;
and likewise, there is no dharma-element, no grasper, and no mind-consciousness.

Likewise, the eyes and so forth do not exist; thus, the jewel of reality, free from the transformations of the eighteen constituents (*dhātu*), should be meditated upon by the yogi. Regarding this, the Blessed One stated in the *Mūlatantra* through the cessation of ignorance and the rest: By the cessation of perishable ignorance (*kṣarāvidyā*), there is the cessation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*); by the cessation of formative forces, there is the cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna*). [4] By the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); by the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). [5]

With the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling. [6] With the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging. [7] With the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence itself, there is the cessation of birth. [8]

Through the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death; that very cessation of the aggregates (skandhas) and elements (dhātus) is known as peace (upaśama). [9] Likewise, through the cessation of the body, there is the cessation of the vital breath (prāṇa); through the cessation of the vital breath, there is the cessation of the bodhicitta.
[10] Through the cessation of the bodhicitta, there is the cessation of emission (cyavana); through the cessation of the moment of emission, there is Buddhahood for all yogins. [11]

Thus, through the cessation of afflictions, there is also the cessation of karma; and through the cessation of karma, there is also the cessation of suffering. [12] Through the cessation of suffering, there would be no arising of afflictions; without the arising of afflictions, the arising of karma never occurs. [13] Without its arising, the arising of suffering is also not found. Free from suffering, the yogi always acts for the benefit of sentient beings. [14]
In this regard, whether impure or even pure, conceptualization gives rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) for sentient beings; from those [afflictions], indeed, karma is born.

[15] From karma, suffering is born, and from that, happiness [arises] again; yet, through the abandonment of the ten wholesome [actions], how will there be happiness? [16] Furthermore, how can there be this accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*) without a mind of suffering and without happiness, [relying] on the imagined deities, mantras, mudrās, and so forth of foolish yogins? [17]

Without merit, how can the accumulation of gnosis arise? Without those two, there is no Buddhahood, nor the supreme state of Vajrasattva. [18] Without that, one's own welfare and the welfare of others do not proceed; yet for you, the pure Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation bodies radiate forth.
[19] When the four states—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth—are blocked along with their causes and fruits, then one is a Buddha, without a doubt. [20]
Free from dust, stainless, immaculate, with faults expelled, and free from affliction; perfectly awakened, self-awakened, the omniscient, the all-knowing Supreme One.
[21] The body of the Lords of Jinas is distinct, due to the cessation of cause and fruit; speech, mind, and bliss are also distinct, as is the body that is a collection of aggregates.

[22] The elements such as earth and so forth are also distinct, as are the objects and the sense faculties; the activities of the organs of action are distinct, as are the organs of action themselves. [23]
"With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands encompassing all.
[24] Thus is the rule of reality in the Root Tantra. Now, for the sake of its accomplishment, the mudrās according to conventional truth are taught in the Abridged Tantra.
Namely: one who knows yoga should always worship, by means of the application of wisdom and skillful means, [his] mother, sister, daughter, and niece.

"Yoga" refers to the unity of the apprehended and the apprehender, the unity of *lalanā* and *rasanā*, and the unity of *caṇḍālī* and semen. Having turned away from that [worldly state], one should worship through celibacy, through imperishable bliss, and through the union of wisdom and means—just like the Lord—by means of the external conventions of place and family regarding the "mother" and so forth.

In the same way, the knower of yoga should always, at all times, worship with the non-emitted bliss (*acyuta-sukha*) by means of the previously mentioned method of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*): the actress, the washerwoman, the *ḍombī*, the outcaste woman, and the Brahmin woman. They should be served with effort so that no separation occurs.
"Separation" in the definitive sense (*nītārtha*) refers to the emission of semen; in the interpretable sense (*neyārtha*), it refers to public ridicule externally.

Therefore, it is the Blessed One’s injunction that one's mother and others should be served with diligence. When service is performed toward the manifest [consorts], suffering is inflicted by royal families and the like upon the beginner yogins; thus, the *mudrās* are called the "five families" for the sake of liberation.

By means of the *vajra*, this is awakening—here, for the sake of liberation, the *mudrā* refers to the five families of the Tathāgatas. Because the mind is sealed (*mudryate*) by this, the *avadhūtī* is called *mudrā*.
Here, by the words "the vajra" and so forth, the mudrās such as the mother and others mentioned in the *Astavyasta* are taken up in their proper order:
here, the mother is Locanā of the Tathāgata family, a Brāhmaṇī, in the navel-lotus;
the sister is Māmakī, the water element, of the Vajra family, a Dombī, in the heart.
The daughter is the fire element (*tejodhātu*), of the Lotus family (*padmakula*), the dancer (*naṭī*) at the throat;
the sister’s daughter is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*), of the Action family (*karmakula*), the washerwoman (*rajakī*) at the forehead;

the wife is Vajradhātvīśvarī, the space element (*ākāśadhātu*), of the Jewel family (*ratnakula*), the outcaste woman (*caṇḍālī*) at the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*); and the low-born woman is the gnosis element (*jñānadhātu*), of the Vajrasattva family (*vajrasattvakula*), at the secret lotus (*guhyakamala*). Thus, this family of the five mudrās above the navel is briefly described. It is said that there are six kinds of families.
The *uṣṇīṣa* is the family of the space element (*ākāśadhātukuḷa*),

the forehead is the family of the wind element (*vāyudhātukuḷa*), the throat is the family of the fire element (*tejodhātukuḷa*), the heart is the family of the water element (*udakadhātukuḷa*), the navel is the family of the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātukuḷa*), and the secret place is the family of the gnosis element (*jñānadhātukuḷa*).
Thus, the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) possesses the quality of space.
Touch is the primary quality of air;
taste is the primary quality of fire;
form is the primary quality of water.
The primary quality of the earth element is odor; the primary quality of the consciousness element is the sound element. Likewise are the ear faculty, the nose faculty, and the body faculty.
the mental faculty, the eye faculty,
and the tongue faculty.
Likewise, there are the organ of speech,
the organ of the hands, and the organ of the feet.
The divine sense organ is the excellent sense organ;
thus is the purification of the mudrā, and thus is the flow of urine and the flow of feces.
Movement, grasping, and speech.
The emission of semen;
thus, among the thirty-six families, six families are to be understood as the thirty-six elements, and likewise the six consciousnesses.
The six formations, the six feelings, and the six perceptions.
The six forms are the six cognitions; thus, the aggregates and elements are seventy-two,
and those deities are doubled as the thirty-six mandala-deities according to the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
The thirty-seventh is Heruka together with Vajravārāhī;
he is the Saṃvara of the body, speech, and mind wheels of that triple family,
and the Saṃvara of the twelve wheels [of the double mandala].

In this *Hevajra Tantra*, the Blessed One stated in the *Cakrasaṃvara* that it is indicated by two lines: "Then the mantra-practitioner should recite the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* twice as much," because of the statement "four times four," the petals,
fields, and so forth, are doubled.
There are four seats (pīṭha), four secondary seats (upapīṭha), and four fields (kṣetra).
There are four secondary fields (*upakṣetra*), four *cchandoha*s, four *upacchandoha*s,
and four *melāpaka*s.

There are four secondary meeting places (*upamelāpaka*), four *pīlava*s, four secondary *pīlava*s (*upapīlava*), four cemeteries (*śmaśāna*), and four secondary cemeteries (*upaśmaśāna*); thus there are twelve stages (*bhūmi*).

For each [stage], there are four Vīreśvarīs together with their Vīras; thus there are forty-eight Yoginīs. In the six wheels: in the space wheel (*ākāśacakra*) are eight Vajra-Ḍākinīs, and in the wind wheel (*vāyucakra*) are eight Khaḍga-Ḍākinīs.
In the fire wheel are eight Ratnaḍākinīs; in the water wheel are eight Padmaḍākinīs;
and in the earth wheel are eight Cakraḍākinīs.

In the wheel of gnosis (*jñānacakra*) are the eight *karttikā*-ḍākinīs; at the [crown] jewel (*vajramaṇi*) are the eight *śūnya*-ḍākinīs who hold single-pronged vajras. Furthermore, in the sixteen cremation grounds are the sixteen ḍākinīs produced from the sixteen joys (*ānanda*). There are two in the pair of ears, two in the nostrils, two in the eyes, two in the tongue and the uvula, two at the door of the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), two at the anus, two at the urinary opening, and two at the opening where semen is emitted.

Thus, among those sixteen yoginīs, the leader is the Blessed Lord Hevajra, who is embraced by Śūnyatā and characterized by innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); he possesses twenty-four arms, doubled [to forty-eight], and abides according to the specific time through the *Ṣaṭcakrasaṃvara*.
By the purification of the year, his body is blue;
by the purification of the solstice (*ayana*), his feet are white and red.
Through purity regarding the three times, he has black, red, and white throats;
time consists of the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa,
and the four ages (yugas) consist of the three-month periods beginning with Capricorn.

Through the purification of that [time], he has four faces—black, red, white, and yellow. Likewise, the six seasons, consisting of two months each beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, are purified as the six aggregates (skandhas) which have the nature of blue, red, and white on the right and left [sides]. Thus, over the twelve months, there are twelve arms—black, red, and white—on the right and left, consisting of four months for each [color].
Thus, by way of the division of the lunar fortnights, there are twenty-four hands;

or, by way of the division of each of the thirty lunar days (*tithi*), there are the joint-pulses (*parvanāḍī*) of the left and right hands, which are the three hundred and sixty finger-joints corresponding to the lunar days of a year. In this manner, Heruka as Kālacakra, who consists of the six families (*ṣaṭkula*), is said to be the *Ādibuddha*.

With a garland of one hundred severed heads—the branches of the hundred Vedas—this Blessed One is the Great Brahmin Kāpālika; thus, the *Ḍākinījālasamvara* is twofold, consisting of six families (*ṣaṭkulātmaka*). In another tantra, it consists of five families (*pañcakulātmaka*). Therefore: "They say the families are of six kinds, but in brief they are fivefold; subsequently they become threefold through the divisions of body, speech, and mind. According to the sequence thus stated, [it refers to] the five families of the five elements, which have the nature of the five aggregates.
"By this, a family (kula) is reckoned and counted; thus it is so designated. This concludes the rule regarding the six families, five families, and three families.
Now, the characteristic of the Tathāgata is stated:
"The glorious one has gone to suchness (tathatā) and has likewise come from it."
"One endowed with this wisdom is called the Tathāgata.

Thus, here, being endowed with this wisdom of emptiness, together with the image of emptiness, he has dwelt within suchness—from the *uṣṇīṣa* in the space element down to the *vajramaṇi*—in the secret lotus on the ground of non-abiding nirvāṇa; that is, in the secret lotuses of the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and [secret place], which are the natures of the elements of wind, fire, water, earth, and gnosis, and which are the *bhagas* of the Vajra-women. Thus the glorious Bodhicittavajra has gone and likewise returned.

Just as he has gone by way of the lower part, so too has he come from the secret lotus of the *vajramaṇi*—the sphere of gnosis—to the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown of the head, with the semen drawn upward. Thus, having gone and returned in this manner, he is perfected through the cessation of the twelve links [of dependent origination] and has attained the twelfth stage (*bhūmi*). Just as he went downward from the forehead according to worldly convention, through the divisions of joy (*ānanda*), supreme joy (*paramānanda*), special joy (*viramānanda*), and innate joy (*sahajānanda*), so too, by way of reversal, through the states of natural outflow (*niṣyanda*), maturation (*vipāka*), human effort (*puruṣakāra*), and purity (*vaimalya*), he has gone from the secret place to the forehead.
And thus it is said: "The outflow (*niṣyanda*) is said to be at the navel; the maturation (*vipāka*) is at the wheel of Dharma;
the virile fruit (*puruṣakāra*) is at the *sambhoga* [wheel]; but the stainlessness (*vaimalya*) is in Great Bliss. Such is the rule to be explained.

Thus, according to the division of the fifteen digits beginning with the first quarter, the gnosis-mind (*jñānacitta*), by its nature as the digit of fullness (*pūrṇākalā*), has gone from the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) to the secret lotus through the conventional downward-flowing semen (*adhoretas*).

Likewise, by the power of yoga, [the seminal essence] is drawn up from the secret lotus through the opening [of the central channel], having reached the forehead lotus in the nature of the full digits (kalās) through the divisions of the digits beginning with the first day of the waxing moon; it reaches the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) in the nature of the sixteenth digit. Thus, for transmigrating beings, the element of passion (*rajodhātu*) goes from the secret place to the crown protuberance through the divisions of the dark first day of the moon and so forth, until at the end of the new moon, it is characterized by the loss of the sixteenth digit.

For the Buddhas, however, that same [essence] is reversed from the crown protuberance and goes to the secret lotus through the divisions of the digits beginning with the first day of the dark fortnight, until at the end of the new moon, it is characterized by the disappearance of the sixteenth lunar digit.

And thus it was said by Samvṛtyādibuddha: "In death for all embodied beings, the lunar nectar (*amṛta*) goes downward and the solar dust (*rajas*) goes upward; [so too] the consciousness (*vijñāna*) of Rāhu [goes upward] at the moment of existence. (SU) "Therefore, O King, the lunar nectar must be made to go upward, and the solar dust and the consciousness of Rāhu [must be made to go] downward into the immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*). In this regard, as will be explained in the *Vivṛti*: "The bodhicitta becomes the moon, consisting of fifteen digits (*kalā*); its form is the vowel (*āli*), the great bliss, and the yoginīs are its parts. This is the rule regarding the sixteen joys (*ṣoḍaśānanda*).
Likewise, in the *Kulapaṭala*, the Blessed One said: "The cause for the arising and abiding of the yoginīs according to their proper order,
their capacity, and their gnosis and consciousness— just as the yoginīs first arise, so too is the cause for the arising of Heruka."
The innate joy (*sahajānanda*), the great bliss, is the syllable *Evaṃ*, the great imperishable.
Thus, when the mind is free from conceptual construction, there is no meditator, nor is there an object of meditation; there is no mantra, nor is there a deity.

Yet both the mantra and the deity exist and abide, by virtue of having a nature free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Precisely by that nature of innate joy, which consists in the subsiding of all stains of conceptual construction, [it exists].

Now, the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate regarding the six aggregates is stated with the words beginning "Vairocana" (cf. HT): here, Vairocana is the leader in the earth-circle, Akṣobhya is the leader in the space-circle, and Amitābha is the leader in the water-circle.
Ratnasambhava is the leader in the fire wheel; Amoghasiddhi is the leader in the wind wheel;
and Sāttvika is the leader in the gnosis wheel.
"And these, respectively, are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sarva, and Vibuddha; they are called the Tattvas.
Thus, according to conventional truth (saṃvṛti), sentient beings have their semen flowing downward."

The Buddhas are so called because of their expansion (*vivṛti*); Brahmā is a Buddha because of his cessation (*nirvṛti*). Viṣṇu is said to be so because he enters (*viśana*) due to the non-excretion of the seminal essence (*vid-dhātu*); that is, because he enters his own body and there is no exit to the exterior, he is called both Buddha and Viṣṇu. Śiva is so called because he is eternally auspicious (*sadā-sukalyāṇa*); "auspicious" refers to unbroken conduct (*akhaṇḍa-śīla*), and because there is no emission of semen (*śukra-cyavana*), he is called both Buddha and Śiva.
Since everyone abides within the self of all,
everyone is Ratnasambhava; because that red element does not undergo emission, there is an absence of suffering.
"Because of the absence of that [craving], there is the end of pleasure and pain; this is the culmination, which is dispassion and the destruction of the substrata.
Thus it is said: "It abides in the Self of all."

Because he possesses the divine eye and the pervasiveness of knowledge of others' minds, the Buddha is called "all. He is "awakened" (*vibuddha*) because of awakening, even without the awakening of the sense faculties such as the eyes (cf.
HT). Amoghasiddhi is the flesh element;
because of its exhaustion, there is an absence of formative factors (*saṃskāra*) for the eyes and so forth.
Due to the absence of that [ignorance], he is awakened (*vibuddha*).

He is the knower of self, the knower of others, all-encompassing, and indeed the most excellent person (*agrapudgala*). Having transcended worldly analogies, he is the supreme lord of knowledge, to be known as the ultimate. Thus it is said: "The rule is that one is called 'awakened' (*buddha*) because of being awakened (*bodhana*), not otherwise."

Reality would consist of true bliss; thus, as it is said in the *Hevajra Tantra*: "The reality that consists of wisdom and means—characterized by the four liberations of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and lack of volitional effort; embraced by the nature of non-referential compassion, loving-kindness, joy, and equanimity; and being untainted (*anāśrava*) and empty—is called Buddhahood. In this way: [he is] one who knows the meaning of truth in twelve aspects and knows reality in sixteen aspects.

"Awakened through the twenty-fold awakening, the Knower of the Ultimate Truth"—thus the Blessed Buddha spoke in this sequence: "The three families, the five families, and the hundred families as one in their essential nature.
Likewise, in the *Nāmasaṃgīti*: "The King of Wrath, six-faced, formidable, six-eyed, six-armed, and powerful;
with fangs bared, skeletal, Halāhala, and hundred-faced."
Likewise: "Terrifying-eyed with vajra-flames, with hair like vajra-flames, vajra-penetration, great penetration, hundred-eyed, vajra-eyed"—this is the rule for the hundred families.

Thus, through the distinction between the concealed (*saṃvṛti*) and the manifest (*vivṛti*), there is the mundane and supramundane reality; that which is with obscuration and that which is without obscuration;
that which has signs and that which is signless.
With conceptual construction and without conceptual construction; superimposed and non-superimposed;
with egoism and without egoism.
For sentient beings and for the Buddhas, [the teaching] arises through the twelvefold dependent origination and arises through the cessation of the twelvefold [links].
Furthermore, it is not explicitly revealed; thus, the restriction regarding all other tantras of the Blessed Buddha should be understood by the wise.

Now, furthermore, by means of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), the deity and so forth are described as "arising in the body" and so on: "Since conventional bliss arises in this body which consists of the five elements, it is therefore called a 'deity' (*devatā*). (Cf. HT:
"He possesses the *bhaga*, thus he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) by the Buddha;
they say there are six kinds of *bhagas*, namely the entirety of the qualities such as sovereignty. Of complete sovereignty, knowledge, fame, glory, [beauty, and renunciation]...")

The word *bhaga* is proclaimed as denoting this quality of good fortune (*saubhāgya*). Alternatively, he is called *Bhagavān* because of his shattering (*bhañjana*) of the Māras such as affliction (*kleśa*).
This is the rule regarding the means (*upāya*) by way of etymological exposition.
Now, wisdom (*prajñā*) is described by the words "the mother" and so forth (cf. HT: "In this context, the means (*upāya*) is the progenitor, the semen-element;
wisdom (*prajñā*) is the mother, the blood-element").

The *ālayavijñāna*—which is presided over by karma and consists of the *gandharva-sattva* at the point of death—is generated as that which pertains to rebirth; this very thing is called "the world" (*jagat*). For the Blessed One has said: "O Sons of the Victor, the triple world is consciousness-only. Since that very world generates the world, Wisdom (*prajñā*) is called the "Mother," while the element of passion (*rajodhātu*) is [the Father]. [As stated in the *Hevajra Tantra*: "Thus, the means (*upāya*) is the semen-element (*śukradhātu*), and she alone is called the 'Sister' (*bhaginī*), because she demonstrates the differentiation. [She shows] the transformation of each individual element: hair, skin, flesh, and blood."
In this way, the means (*upāya*) is the brother, for from the division of the channels, bones, and marrow, the semen-element (*śukradhātu*) arises.
She herself is called the daughter (*duhitā*) because she milks the qualities (*guṇa*);

by the word "quality" are meant the objects of sound, touch, taste, form, smell, and the dharma-element, and she is so called because she milks—that is, apprehends—them. Thus, the means is the son, for since it is the activity of the eyes and so forth, it is the element of means (*upāyadhātu*).

In this way, wisdom (prajñā) is called the sister’s daughter because she is the engagement of the consciousnesses with respect to objects; and means (upāya) is called the brother’s son because he is the engagement in the eyes and so forth. Thus, wisdom is called the wife because she is the engagement in the bliss of emission (cyavana); means is also called the husband.
This is because both possess the nature of the bliss of emission through their mutual dependence upon one another.

From detachment (*virāga*), that which arises at the end of the contact with wisdom (*prajñāsparśāntaja*) is called the means (*upāya*); such is the rule for the six mudrās. From the delusion (*mohana*) of all elements (*dhātu*), she is designated as the Brāhmaṇī.

Wisdom is called *rajakī* (the dyer) because of her coloring; she is a *nartakī* (dancer) because of her flickering nature. She is known as *caṇḍālinī* (the outcaste woman) because of her burning, and is remembered as *ḍombinī* (the low-caste woman) because of her touch.

In this way, the means (*upāya*) should also be understood through its fivefold functional nature. Thus, all this is [described] externally; therefore, it is conceptualized by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) following the Vedas and other traditions that all women and all men are born of a single human species, and they maintain that there is no other caste for them—so it is held in all the Tantras.

Now, the recitation of mantras and so forth by way of the nature of the elements is described with the words "speech" (*jalpana*) and so on. Here, the speech of all sentient beings—the speech of vowels and consonants (*āli-kāli*)—is called *japa* because it is speech; thus, for those practicing the yoga of reality, the mandala is likewise the drawing [of lines] under the feet. It is called a mandala because the earth is marked by the two feet. Likewise, the clapping of hands is a mudrā, as is the snapping of the fingers.
Thus, for sentient beings, that which is thought is itself the object of meditation (*dhyeya*) for yogins through the knowledge of others' minds.

Since that object of meditation is "thinking," therefore the non-thinking (*acintana*) is the object of meditation for yogins. Consequently, whatever pleasure a sentient being attains in relation to the father—whether at the end of death or at the moment of rebirth—that very same pleasure is experienced by the male himself until the age of sixteen; by the female, it is experienced until the age of twelve.

That very bliss by which transmigrating beings experience death, birth, and stability within cyclic existence, is called the "meditative absorption" (*dhyāna*) of yogins when it becomes stabilized during the state of passing away. By me, Vajragarbha, this entire summary of the condensed meaning of each chapter has been taught within the five chapters from the *Hevajra* tantra, which consists of five hundred thousand verses, specifically from its middle portion of one hundred thousand verses.
Beyond this, the chapter on conduct (*caryā*) and the others are to be understood in detail.

The summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) is [given] by thirty verses from the first hundred thousand [verses] in the Chapter on the Family; by forty verses from the second hundred thousand in the Chapter on Mantra;
by twenty-four verses from the third hundred thousand in the Chapter on the Deities;
by six verses from the fourth hundred thousand in the Chapter on Initiation; and by twenty verses from the fifth hundred thousand in the Chapter on Reality.
Thus, by means of this commentary, the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*) across the five chapters should be understood by yogins through these one hundred and twenty verses.

Thus ends the "Great Chapter on the Exposition of Reality" (*tattvanirdeśo mahoddeśaḥ*) in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā-hevajra-ṭīkā*. Thus concludes the commentary on the summary meaning of the chapter on reality. || 0 ||
Pacified, the destruction of existence and non-existence, the all-pervasive Lord, inseparable from emptiness and compassion.

"Beneficial in the beginning, in the middle, and in the end," Vajragarbha composes a commentary on the fifth chapter—a commentary that teaches the *tattva* of the Buddhas for the benefit of all sentient beings and for the attainment of the fruit of Mahāmudrā, which is Great Bliss.

At this point the Blessed One said: "Now we shall illustrate the chapter concerning reality (*tattva*), which begins with the words: 'According to their own nature... (HT 1.5.1). Their own nature (*svarūpa*) is the Tathāgata’s gnosis, which is self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedaka*)."

By virtue of this intrinsic nature—which is free from perceived objects, perception, and a perceiving subject, and from the transformation of the eighteen elements—there exists for yogins neither (1) an external "form," nor (2) a "seer," nor (3) a visual consciousness; nor (4) "sound," (5) a "hearer," nor (6) an auditory consciousness; nor (7) "odor," (8) a "smeller," and...

(9) olfactory consciousness; (10) taste, (11) the taster, and (12) gustatory consciousness; (13) touch, (14) the toucher, and (15) tactile consciousness; (16) the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), (17) the perceiving subject, and (18) mental consciousness.
Likewise, the sense-faculties, beginning with the eye, also do not exist.

In this manner, by severing the sequence beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), the yogin must meditate upon the Jewel of True Reality (*dharmaratna*), which is free from transformation by the eighteen constituents (*dhātu*) mentioned above.
As the Blessed One stated in the Root Tantra (*Pañcalakṣahevajra*):

Through the cessation of ignorance, which is subject to change (*kṣara*), there is the cessation of volition; through the cessation of volition, the cessation of primary awareness (*vijñāna*); through the cessation of primary awareness, the cessation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Through the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the sixfold sphere of the senses; through the cessation of the sixfold sphere of the senses, there is the cessation of contact; through the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling.
Through the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving;
through the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming.
Through the cessation of becoming, there is the cessation of birth; through the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of aging and death.
The cessation of the aggregates and the elements is traditionally conceived as peace.
Thus, through the "interruption" of the body, there is also the "interruption" of the vital breath;
through the "interruption" of the vital breath, the "interruption" of the bodhicitta;
and through the "interruption" of the bodhicitta, the "interruption" of emission (*cyavana*).
All yogins attain Buddhahood through the "interruption" of the moment of emission.

Thus, through the "interruption" of the afflictions (*kleśa*), there is the "interruption" of karma (*karman*); through the "interruption" of karma, there is the "interruption" of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Afflictions no longer arise due to the "interruption" of suffering. (15) The virtuous and non-virtuous [actions] of sentient beings would be mere conceptual constructions.
(16) Since suffering has arisen from karma, how could there be happiness?
How could there be happiness from abandoning the ten wholesome paths of action?
17. How can the mind of the lords of yoga become blissful? How can one be endowed with merit?
And how does [the deity] arise through mantras, mudrās, and so forth?
18. How may the equipment of knowledge arise? How may it belong to Vajrasattva? 19. How does the welfare of oneself and others increase?
20. He whose fourth [nature] is realized is the Buddha. 21. Liberated from passion and the like, he is pure and of stainless nature.
22–23. By the power of cause and fruit, the forms of the Lords of Jinas come into being.
24. "With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, with ears everywhere in the world, it stands encompassing all.
The knower of yoga should constantly worship that through knowledge, by means of skillful methods and proper conduct.
Yoga is union; it is the union of *lalanā* and *rasanā*.
It is the union with *Caṇḍālī*. One should worship knowledge through the method of means (*upāya*) according to the rule.
[The women are] the actress, the washerwoman, the *Ḍombī*, the *Caṇḍālī*, and the Brahmin woman.
Knowledge [is attained] through means and method;
there would be no distinction [between them].
One should worship.
The mudrās are known as the five families; thus, the five mudrā families are mentioned. The six families are also taught.

6) There is the expulsion of urine and excrement, as well as errors in grasping and speaking. One should recite the *ḍākinī-cakra*. Therein, the Lord Hevajra is embraced by coemergent bliss (*sahajānanda*) and emptiness. It is called a "family" (*kula*) because of the gathering of the five aggregates and the five elements; thus it is called a family. [He is] the Tathāgata. Rāhu enters the mouth of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Bodhicitta is the moon, consisting of fifteen digits; great bliss has the form of the vowels, and the yoginīs arise from the parts of the moon. Thus, the cause is the nature of the support for the arising of the yoginīs. The cause for the attainment of the yoginīs is, from the beginning, the birth of Heruka. Thus, the imperishable coemergent bliss is the supreme and ultimate great bliss. There is no meditator and no object of meditation; there is neither mantra nor deity. Mantra and deity are indeed of a non-conceptual form. Vairocana is the sovereign in the mandala of earth; Akṣobhya is the sovereign in space; Amitābha is the sovereign in water; Ratnasambhava is the sovereign in fire; Amoghasiddhi is the sovereign in wind. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sarva, and Vibuddha are said to be the reality (*tattva*). Three families, five families, one nature—even a hundred—[are taught]. In the *Nāmasaṅgīti*, the wrathful kings are described as six-faced, formidable, six-eyed, six-armed, heroic, a mass of bones, displaying his teeth, with poison like *halāhala* in hundreds of mouths. And likewise: the vajra-blazing luster, the vajra-blazing eyes, the vajra-hair, the vajra-penetration, the great penetration, hundreds of vajra-eyes, [vajra-]eyes. From the worldly perspective, from the perspective of the leader, from the perspective of reality, from the external and internal, from the afflicted and the unafflicted, the characteristic of perception, the characteristic of self, conceptual and non-conceptual, with superimposition and without superimposition, with ego and without ego, from the perspective of sentient beings, from the perspective of the Buddha, from the twelve links of dependent origination, and from the cessation of the twelve links—not only from the perspective of reality, but in all tantras it is stated that the training of the wise arises in the body; the fortunate one is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*), therefore he is called the Blessed One. It is said that there are six qualities such as sovereignty. Because of crushing Māra and others, he is the Blessed One in reality. Skillful means (*upāya*) is explained here through the mother and so forth, while wisdom (*prajñā*) is explained through the father, who is the consideration of semen. Like karma, the *gandharva-sattva* and the *ālayavijñāna* are born; thus the world dies through birth, as proclaimed by the Blessed One. Oṃ! The sons of the Victors, the three realms, are mere representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*); they generate the world. The mother is the blood; through division, the sister is the skin, flesh, and blood—the transformation of the elements. The brother is the semen, the royal path. Because of milking the bone and semen, she is the daughter; the sound, external scent, and taste are the sisters. Because of milking the *dharmadhātu*, since one experiences it, she is like the son of skillful means; the eye-delusions are the sisters and daughters; the eye-ignorance and eye-knowledge are the wife through fortune, and the husband through union.

Because they are free from desire (*niṣkāmatva*), they are untouchable (*asparśā*); the methods (*upāya*) are born of the end; the seals (*mudrā*) are entirely external. The *brāhmaṇī*, *rajakī*, *raktī*, and *nartakī* arise from conduct (*varttana*); the *caṇḍālī* and *ḍombinī* are the knowers of reality (*tatvajñā*). The method is extensive externally; all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are the woman (*strī*). "Born previously," "speech," and so forth, refer to the mantra, the elements (*dhātu*), and the voice; the recitation (*jāpa*) is *ālikālī*. The "lotus-mandala" (*padamaṇḍala*) is the mandala of rubbing (*malana*). The hand-seal (*hastamudrā*) is the mental contemplation (*cittavicintana*); contemplation is non-contemplation (*acintana*). Death and liberation, semen (*śukra*), and the play of passion (*rāgakrīḍā*). [From] the *Pañcalakṣahevajra*, the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*, the *Hevajratantra*.
My speech is virtuous in the beginning, the middle, and the end;
it is the *Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra*. From that [tantra], the knower of yoga, the lord of definitive accomplishment, has emerged as one who possesses the accomplished Lord.

*The Secret of the Net of Ṭākinīs*. Thus it was said by Vajragarbha: "The procedure for worship as taught in the Root Tantra is as follows: the knower of yoga should always worship according to the method of wisdom and means. 'Yoga' refers to the unity of Caṇḍālī and semen; therefore, one turns away from that. Having turned away from that, the knower of yoga should always worship with the lord—that is, with the immutable bliss of celibacy—according to the method of wisdom and means at all times, through non-emitted bliss. Therefore, having turned away from that, one turns away from that.
